Slide 1

NEUROSURGERY LECTURE SERIES · YEAR 5

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

From clinical signs to anatomical diagnosis

Thursday, September 3 · 1:00 – 2:00 PM

Dr. Sara Alsulaimani · Department of Surgery, Neurosurgery Unit

Slide 2

ROADMAP

Learning Objectives

Describe the basic anatomical organization of the brain relevant to localization of intracranial lesions.

1

Recognize common signs and symptoms of intracranial tumors, including features of raised intracranial pressure.

2

Correlate neurological findings with the likely anatomical location of an intracranial tumor.

3

4

Differentiate the typical clinical presentations of tumors involving the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, cerebellar, and sellar regions.

Outline the role of CT and MRI in localizing and characterizing intracranial tumors.

5

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

1

Slide 3

CLINICAL REASONING

Why Localization Matters

Mass effect

The clinical exam is a localizing tool

Displacement & compression of adjacent structures

  • A tumor’s signs and symptoms mirror the function of the brain tissue it disturbs.
  • History + examination generate an anatomical hypothesis before any scan is obtained.
  • That hypothesis focuses imaging review and helps explain findings that don’t fit — e.g. a “false localizing” sixth-nerve palsy from raised ICP.
  • Localization also anticipates the functional risk of surgery in that region.

Infiltration / destruction

Direct loss of the function that region performs

Irritation

Abnormal cortical discharge → seizures

Signs a tumor produces depend on WHERE it is, HOW FAST it grows, and its effect on surrounding tissue.

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

2

  • Brain tumour suspected — the study to perform primarily → CT scan. mx 429 ×3
Notes

Principles of Localization

Goal
Use history + neurological examination before imaging to predict where the lesion is → then correlate with CT/MRI. Tumor manifestations usually mirror the normal function of the affected region (motor, sensory, language, vision, memory, behavior, seizures…).
Notes

Why a clinical hypothesis matters

1 · Directs imaging Guides how the CT/MRI is read.·2 · Tests the fit Do the imaging findings actually explain the deficits?·3 · Plans surgery Especially near eloquent cortex.

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

3

Slide 5

NEUROANATOMY

Principles of Functional Localization

Eloquent vs. non-eloquent cortex

Eloquent areas (motor strip, language, primary visual/sensory cortex) produce deficits when damaged; “silent” areas (e.g. right frontal/temporal pole) may grow large before symptoms appear.

Hemispheric dominance

Language localizes to the dominant hemisphere (left in ~95% of right-handers) — explains why left temporal/frontal lesions cause aphasia and right-sided ones cause neglect.

Cortex vs. white matter tracts

A lesion can disconnect distant regions by interrupting a tract (e.g. optic radiations, arcuate fasciculus) without directly involving the cortex it affects.

Homuncular organization

The motor and sensory strips are somatotopically mapped — a focal deficit (e.g. face-arm predominant) points to a specific point along the strip.

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

4

  • 60-year-old, progressive left-sided weakness (arm > leg) over 3 months + left UMN facial palsy, normal speech → right frontal glioblastoma (progressive = tumour; sudden = stroke). mx 434 ×2
Notes

Always consider

Side Right vs left·Dominant vs non-dominant Language is left-dominant in most people, incl. >70% of left-handers; a minority right/bilateral·Cortex vs white matter Different functions & pathology (e.g. MS = mainly white matter)
Eloquent vs silent cortex
Eloquent cortex = functionally critical area where damage causes a major deficit (primary motor cortex, language cortex, primary visual cortex). Silent / non-eloquent regions → a tumor can grow large before causing a focal deficit.

Added explanationRoot levels to know: C5 = shoulder abduction, biceps reflex, lateral arm (regimental badge) · C6 = lateral forearm + thumb, brachioradialis · C7 = middle finger, triceps · C8/T1 = little finger/medial forearm · T4 = nipple, T10 = umbilicus · L4 = knee jerk, medial leg · L5 = big-toe extension (EHL), lateral leg, dorsum of foot · S1 = plantar flexion, ankle jerk, lateral foot, posterior thigh/calf. A disc usually compresses the lower root at that level (L4–L5 disc → L5 root; L5–S1 disc → S1 root).
  • Pain to the buttock, back of thigh and lateral foot, sensory loss lateral leg/foot and posterior thigh, loss of plantar flexion → L5–S1 (S1 root). 437 ×8
  • Urinary retention, two months of posterior-thigh pain, bilateral foot drop, lateral-foot sensory loss, decreased anal tone → cauda equina syndrome. 437 ×5
Slide 6

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

How a Tumor Produces Symptoms

Mass effect & edema

Infiltration / destruction

Direct compression and surrounding vasogenic edema distort adjacent, otherwise normal, brain.

Diffusely growing tumors (e.g. glioma) replace and destroy functioning tissue directly.

Cortical irritation

CSF pathway obstruction

Abnormal electrical discharge from tumor margin presents as focal or secondarily generalized seizures.

Tumors near ventricles/aqueduct/fourth ventricle cause obstructive hydrocephalus → raised ICP.

Notes

Mechanisms compared

MechanismWhat happensClinical / surgical meaning
Mass effectCompresses or displaces normal tissue rather than destroying it; white-matter tracts remain intactDeficits may recover after decompression / removal
Infiltration & destructionMalignant cells invade cortex and white matter (as in glioma)Cannot be cleanly separated from functional tissue → resection may destroy working brain/tracts
Cortical irritationIrritation of the cortex (not white matter alone)Cortical tumors commonly present with seizures
ObstructionCSF pathway blocked: 3rd-ventricle lesion, ventricular compression, mass near 4th ventricleHydrocephalus → raised ICP (headache, vomiting); may unmask a previously silent large tumor
Presentation depends on: tumor location · growth rate · degree of compression / infiltration · effect on surrounding tissue and CSF pathways.
Slide 7

RAISED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE

The Monro–Kellie Doctrine

The skull is a fixed-volume box. Brain + blood + CSF must sum to a constant — growth of a tumor (or its edema) must be compensated, or pressure rises.

Brain tissue

Blood

CSF

~80%

~10%

~10%

Displaced by mass effect; compresses last and abruptly once other buffers are exhausted.

CSF and venous blood are displaced first — the earliest compensatory buffer.

Absorption increases and volume shifts into the spinal thecal sac.

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

6

  • Tumour patient collapses with high ICP — the pressure–volume relationship → keyed "the curve shifts to the right" (he is on the steep, decompensated part where a small extra volume causes a big rise in pressure). mx 438
  • Cannot extend the big toe → L4–L5 (L5 root). 435
Notes

Raised Intracranial Pressure

Monro–Kellie doctrine

Brain tissue · 80%Blood 10%CSF 10%
The adult skull is a fixed, rigid compartment. An increase in one component (tumor, blood, CSF) without adequate compensation → raised ICP → deterioration / herniation. Infants differ: the skull is not yet completely rigid.
Slide 8

RAISED ICP

Clinical Features to Recognize

Headache

Sixth (abducens) nerve palsy

Worse in the morning, with coughing/straining (Valsalva), or when lying flat

A "false localizing sign" — long intracranial course makes CN VI vulnerable to pressure, independent of tumor site

Vomiting

Cushing triad

Often without preceding nausea, may be projectile

Hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration — a late, pre-terminal sign of impending herniation

Papilledema

Declining consciousness

Blurred disc margins on fundoscopy — always examine the fundus

From drowsiness to coma as compensation fails — a neurosurgical emergency

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

7

Notes

True vs false localizing signs

True localizing signFalse localizing sign
Deficit caused directly by dysfunction of the involved anatomical regionDeficit caused by a distant effect (raised ICP / hydrocephalus) — does not point to the site of the tumor
e.g. contralateral weakness from a precentral lesionCN VI palsy: this nerve is especially vulnerable to pressure/stretch → does not necessarily mean a lesion at the CN VI nucleus/brainstem
Notes

Raised ICP syndrome

Severe headache
Worse in the morning
Worse with coughing / straining
May worsen lying flat
Vomiting
Blurred vision
Possible CN VI palsy
↓ level of consciousness in advanced cases
  • Early-morning headache of raised ICP → increased systemic PCO₂ (hypoventilation during sleep → cerebral vasodilatation). mx 434 ×2
Notes

Other manifestations of an intracranial tumor

Motor disturbance / weakness
Hyperreflexia
Aphasia
Personality / behavioral change
Numbness / sensory disturbance
Headache · vomiting
Seizures
Blurred vision
Cognitive decline / dementia
Reduced consciousness
Cushing triad
EXAM
Marks severe / late raised ICP with a high risk of neurological deterioration or death. Recognize the cause before this stage.
The three components were not listed in the lecture notes — added here as standard content.
Hypertension (wide pulse pressure)·Bradycardia·Irregular respiration
Acute deterioration = neurosurgical emergency
Large hemorrhage or severe raised ICP → sudden drowsiness / ↓ consciousness. ABC → urgent CT. Any new seizure or focal deficit with suspected intracranial pathology → brain imaging is required.
  • Cushing's triad = high systolic BP (wide pulse pressure), low HR, low/irregular RR. mx 432
  • Numbness up to the nipple (pinprick) → T4 sensory level. 437
Added explanationMyelopathy vs radiculopathy: cord compression (myelopathy) gives UMN signs below the level — clumsy hands, loss of fine movement, unsteady/spastic gait, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign, sensory level, sphincters late. Root compression (radiculopathy) gives LMN signs in one root — dermatomal pain/numbness, weakness, lost reflex. Cauda equina = LMN, saddle anaesthesia, retention, ↓anal tone.
Added explanationNeurogenic shock (cord injury above ~T6): loss of sympathetic tone → hypotension with bradycardia (or an inappropriately normal HR) and warm, dry peripheries. Treat with IV fluids, then vasopressors; always exclude haemorrhage first. Steroids (methylprednisolone) are no longer routinely recommended.
  • Fall from height, thoracic tenderness, paraplegia, BP 85/45, pulse 50 → neurogenic shock. 441 ×12
Slide 9

PRESENTING SIGN

Seizure Semiology Can Suggest Location

  • A new-onset focal seizure in an adult should always raise suspicion for a structural lesion.
  • Focal seizures may remain focal (retained awareness or altered awareness) or secondarily generalize.
  • The seizure semiology — what the patient/witness describes — often points directly to the lobe of origin.

Frontal

Motor jerking, head/eye version, brief with rapid recovery, prominent nocturnal clusters

Temporal

Aura (déjà vu, epigastric rising, fear, olfactory/gustatory), oral automatisms, behavioral arrest

Parietal

Contralateral sensory disturbance, tingling or distorted body perception

Occipital

Elementary visual hallucinations (flashing lights, colors), forced eye deviation

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

8

Notes

Tumor-Related Seizures

A focal seizure may remain focal, occur with intact awareness, or progress to secondary generalization (e.g. mouth twitching or one-arm twitching). History is critical — seizure semiology itself localizes the lesion.
LobeSeizure semiologyClue
FrontalPrimarily motor: jerking, head deviationBrief, rapid; often occur at night
TemporalMotor or non-motor: déjà vu, strange / emotional experiences, repetitive movements (automatisms), abdominal sensationHighly epileptogenic lobe
ParietalContralateral sensory phenomena: tingling; distorted sensation / body perception (limb feels swollen or twisted)No obvious jerking needed
OccipitalVisual phenomena: flashing lights, visual hallucinations (objects/animals not really there)Visual symptoms only
  • Middle finger sensation → C7. 438 ×2
Slide 10

REGIONAL LOCALIZATION

Frontal Lobe

Tumor Presentation

Anatomy & Function

  • Contralateral hemiparesis, often face/arm predominant
  • Personality and behavioral change — disinhibition, apathy, poor judgment (may mimic psychiatric illness)
  • Expressive (Broca’s) aphasia if dominant hemisphere involved
  • Gait apraxia and urinary incontinence with bifrontal/medial lesions
  • Anosmia with orbitofrontal masses (e.g. olfactory groove meningioma)
  • Contralateral gaze deviation from frontal eye field involvement
  • Precentral gyrus = primary motor cortex (somatotopic homunculus)
  • Broca’s area (dominant, posterior inferior frontal gyrus) → speech production
  • Prefrontal cortex → executive function, judgment, personality, social behavior
  • Frontal eye fields → conjugate gaze
  • Orbitofrontal region lies against the olfactory tract

Personality change is easy to misattribute to mood or psychiatric disorder — always consider a frontal mass.

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

9

Personality change is easy to misattribute to mood or psychiatric disorder — always consider a frontal mass.
Notes

Frontal lobe

StructureFunctionLesion produces
Precentral gyrusPrimary motor cortex (both hemispheres)Contralateral hemiparesis (right lesion → left weakness)
Supplementary motor areaMotor association; superior / medial frontalMotor-association deficit
Broca area dominant F3Speech production (inferior frontal gyrus: pars opercularis + pars triangularis; third division = pars orbitalis)Expressive / Broca aphasia; surgical injury → major language deficit
Prefrontal cortexExecutive function, judgment, social inhibition, appropriate behaviorDisinhibition, apathy, poor judgment, personality change
Frontal eye fieldConjugate gazeGaze abnormality / deviation
Orbitofrontal / olfactory tractSmellAnosmia
Bifrontal clue
Gait apraxia + urinary incontinence → particularly suggestive of bifrontal involvement.
Psychiatric vs organic
New psychiatric or personality symptoms can be caused by a frontal tumor — consider an organic cause before labeling the symptoms purely psychiatric.
Slide 11

REGIONAL LOCALIZATION

Parietal Lobe

Tumor Presentation

Anatomy & Function

  • Contralateral cortical sensory loss — impaired two-point discrimination, graphesthesia, stereognosis
  • Dominant: Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right confusion); ideomotor apraxia; alexia
  • Non-dominant: hemispatial neglect, anosognosia, constructional apraxia
  • Inferior contralateral homonymous quadrantanopia (superior optic radiation)
  • Postcentral gyrus = primary somatosensory cortex
  • Dominant (usually left) — language integration, calculation, praxis
  • Non-dominant (usually right) — spatial awareness & attention
  • Optic radiation fibers loop through the parietal lobe (superior fibers)

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

10

Notes

Parietal lobe

Dominant parietalNon-dominant parietal
RoleLanguage integration; writing, calculation / organization, sensory integrationSpatial awareness (no weakness)
LesionGerstmann syndromeContralateral hemispatial neglect, spatial disorientation, agnosia, constructional apraxia
Key point—Normal motor power, yet cannot navigate or interact with the contralateral side of space
Gerstmann syndrome — dominant parietal
MCQ
Agraphia
Acalculia
Finger agnosia
Left–right confusion
Cortical sensory loss (postcentral gyrus = primary somatosensory cortex)
Contralateral loss of higher sensory integration, tested at the bedside by: two-point discrimination · graphesthesia · stereognosis. The patient may feel a basic stimulus but cannot interpret it.
Optic radiations
EXAM
The superior optic radiations pass through the parietal region → parietal lesion = contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia.
Slide 12

REGIONAL LOCALIZATION

Temporal Lobe

Tumor Presentation

Anatomy & Function

  • Receptive aphasia (fluent but nonsensical/paraphasic speech) if dominant hemisphere
  • Short-term memory impairment with mesial temporal involvement
  • Complex partial (focal impaired-awareness) seizures with auras — déjà vu, epigastric rising sensation, olfactory/gustatory hallucinations, automatisms
  • Superior contralateral homonymous quadrantanopia — classic "pie in the sky" (Meyer’s loop)
  • Contralateral facial/visual recognition difficulty with select lesions
  • Wernicke’s area (dominant, posterior superior temporal gyrus) → language comprehension
  • Hippocampus & mesial structures → memory consolidation
  • Primary auditory cortex (Heschl’s gyrus)
  • Meyer’s loop — inferior optic radiation fibers sweep through the temporal lobe

Temporal lobe

Wernicke areaLanguage comprehension (dominant temporal)Receptive aphasia
Arcuate fasciculusWhite-matter link between Broca and WernickePart of the language network

  • Seizure + enhancing lesion of the left inferior frontal lobe → difficulty in expression (Broca / expressive aphasia). mx 437
Notes

Broca vs Wernicke aphasia

Broca (expressive)Wernicke (receptive)
LocationDominant inferior frontal gyrus (F3)Dominant temporal lobe
SpeechExpressive dysfunction (production impaired)Fluent but meaningless / inappropriate
ComprehensionRelatively preservedImpaired; answers fluently with unrelated content

Visual field defects by lesion site

EXAM

LesionPictureDefect
Sellar / chiasmBitemporal hemianopia — classic sellar defect
Slide 13

REGIONAL LOCALIZATION

Occipital Lobe

Tumor Presentation

Anatomy & Function

  • Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, classically with macular sparing (dual blood supply/bilateral pole representation)
  • Elementary visual hallucinations — unformed flashes, shapes, colors (vs. the complex hallucinations of temporal lesions)
  • Anton syndrome (cortical blindness with denial/confabulation) if bilateral occipital involvement
  • Usually preserved motor, sensory, and language function — a relatively "silent" region outside vision
  • Primary visual cortex lines the calcarine sulcus
  • Macular (central) vision has bilateral cortical representation at the occipital pole
  • Association visual cortex → higher-order visual processing

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

12

Notes

Occipital lobe

FindingDetail
Primary functionVision (primary + association visual cortex)
Classic lesionContralateral homonymous hemianopia, classically with macular sparing
Association cortexImpaired visual recognition
SeizuresFlashing lights, visual hallucinations
Occipital lesions can produce major visual symptoms without prominent motor, sensory or language deficits.
Anton syndrome
Occipital cortical damage (tumor, trauma, infiltration…) → cortical blindness. The patient cannot see but confabulates and behaves as if vision were intact.
Slide 14

REGIONAL LOCALIZATION

Cerebellum & Posterior Fossa

Tumor Presentation

Anatomy & Function

  • Ipsilateral limb ataxia, dysmetria (past-pointing), intention tremor — hemispheric lesions
  • Truncal/gait ataxia, wide-based gait — vermian lesions (common in children, e.g. medulloblastoma)
  • Nystagmus, dysarthria (scanning speech), hypotonia
  • Early obstructive hydrocephalus → raised ICP presents sooner than in supratentorial tumors
  • Cranial nerve palsies (V–VIII) or long tract signs if the brainstem is compressed
  • Cerebellar hemispheres → coordination of ipsilateral limb movement
  • Vermis (midline) → truncal/axial coordination and gait
  • Fourth ventricle lies just anterior — small masses here obstruct CSF flow early
  • Brainstem and lower cranial nerves are close neighbors

Posterior fossa masses cause raised ICP disproportionately early because of proximity to the fourth ventricle.

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

13

Posterior fossa masses cause raised ICP disproportionately early because of proximity to the fourth ventricle.
  • 10-year-old girl, headache + unstable gait, past-pointing and pendular reflexes → medulloblastoma of the cerebellum. mx 432 ×5
  • 6-year-old, headache, vomiting, frequent falls, midline posterior fossa tumour → differential medulloblastoma, ependymoma, (pilocytic) astrocytoma. mx 439
  • "Loss of fine movement" (incomplete recall) → keyed "spinal level" — the lesion is in the cord (myelopathy). 439
  • Child with neck pain 2 weeks after trauma (X-ray) → atlanto-axial subluxation. 437
Notes

Cerebellum & Posterior Fossa

Tight compartment → EARLY raised ICP
The posterior fossa holds the cerebellum, brainstem, 4th ventricle and important neurovascular structures, with little room to expand. A growing mass quickly compresses the brainstem and 4th ventricle → early obstructive hydrocephalus, so ICP rises disproportionately early. These tumors are particularly seen in children.
ComponentFunction / lesion
Cerebellum (overall)Coordinates and smooths movement → lesion = impaired coordination
Cerebellar hemisphereLimb coordination: dysmetria, limb ataxia
VermisAxial / truncal control → truncal ataxia: cannot sit unsupported, cannot stand, postural instability
Brainstem involvementCN V–VIII palsies or long-tract signs
Common findings — know for the exam
EXAM
Truncal / limb ataxia
Wide-based gait
Dysmetria
Nystagmus
Scanning / abnormal dysarthria
Early obstructive hydrocephalus
Slide 15

REGIONAL LOCALIZATION

Sellar & Parasellar Region

Tumor Presentation

Anatomy & Function

  • Bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression (classic sellar visual field defect)
  • Endocrine dysfunction — hypopituitarism (fatigue, hypogonadism) or hormone excess (e.g. prolactinoma → amenorrhea/galactorrhea; acromegaly; Cushing disease)
  • Headache from dural stretch, independent of a discrete raised-ICP mechanism
  • Cavernous sinus extension → ophthalmoplegia (CN III/IV/VI) and facial numbness (V1/V2)
  • Pituitary apoplexy: sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia — a neurosurgical emergency
  • Pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica, capped by the optic chiasm
  • Cavernous sinuses flank the sella — contain CN III, IV, VI and V1/V2
  • Anterior pituitary secretes ACTH, TSH, GH, LH/FSH, prolactin
  • Posterior pituitary stores ADH and oxytocin

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

14

  • Pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm (visual loss + disturbed menses) → bitemporal hemianopia. mx 437 ×6
  • Headache, visual changes and bilateral milky nipple discharge → serum TSH and prolactin. mx 441
Notes

Sellar / Pituitary Region

Localization matters here because of the critical structures that surround the pituitary.

Cavernous sinusContains the internal carotid artery and CN III, IV, V1, V2, VICritical neurovascular neighbors
Endocrine tissue ProlactinomaHormone hypersecretion or hyposecretionHypopituitarism (fatigue, hypogonadism) or excess: prolactinoma, acromegaly, Cushing disease
PatientPresentation
FemaleMenstrual irregularity (amenorrhea / galactorrhea)

Lobe-by-Lobe Signatures

  • Hyperextension injury with C5 and C6 root injury → sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the arm and forearm. 437
Slide 17

IMAGING

The Role of CT

Fast, widely available, and excellent for bone and acute hemorrhage — the first-line study in the emergency setting.

When it is used first

What it shows well

Limitations

  • Acute presentation — new focal deficit, seizure, depressed consciousness
  • Suspected raised ICP or herniation before further workup
  • Trauma, or when MRI is unavailable/contraindicated
  • Acute hemorrhage, calcification, bone erosion/hyperostosis
  • Hydrocephalus and midline shift
  • Gross mass effect and edema (with contrast for enhancement)
  • Lower soft-tissue contrast than MRI
  • Posterior fossa/brainstem obscured by beam-hardening artifact
  • Ionizing radiation, iodinated contrast risk (renal function, allergy)

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

16

Notes

Imaging & Emergency Approach

Clinical localization comes first; imaging then confirms and characterizes the suspected lesion. Do not assign detailed function from the CT appearance alone — always correlate with the clinical findings.
CTMRI
RoleFirst-line in emergencies: fast, widely availableDefinitive study: superior soft- tissue contrast + multiplanar
Shows wellAcute hemorrhage, calcification, bone erosion / hyperostosis, hydrocephalus + midline shift, gross mass effect + edema (contrast CT: enhancement)Tumor characterization & surgical planning; posterior fossa / brainstem; functional mapping near eloquent cortex
LimitsLower soft-tissue contrast; posterior fossa / brainstem obscured by beam-hardening artifact; ionizing radiation; iodinated contrast risk (renal dysfunction, allergy)Contraindicated in some patients (e.g. pacemaker); less suited to rapid emergency triage
Slide 18

IMAGING

The Role of MRI

Superior soft-tissue contrast and multiplanar imaging make MRI the definitive study for characterizing and surgically planning around a tumor.

T1 ± gadolinium contrast

Anatomy; enhancement pattern suggests blood-brain-barrier breakdown / tumor grade

T2 / FLAIR

Edema, infiltration, and non-enhancing tumor extent (FLAIR suppresses CSF signal)

DWI / ADC

Restricted diffusion — helps distinguish abscess, lymphoma, or highly cellular tumor

GRE / SWI

Blood products and calcification (susceptibility artifact)

Advanced: perfusion, spectroscopy, fMRI, tractography

Grading, metabolic profile, and pre-surgical mapping of eloquent cortex/white matter tracts

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

17

Notes

MRI sequences

SequenceWhat it tells you
T1 ± gadoliniumAnatomy + enhancement → blood–brain barrier breakdown; suggests tumor grade
T2 / FLAIREdema, infiltration, non-enhancing tumor extent (FLAIR suppresses CSF signal)
DWI / ADCRestricted diffusion → helps separate abscess, lymphoma, highly cellular tumors
GRE / SWIBlood products and calcification (susceptibility artifact)
  • Intra-axial heterogeneous enhancing lesion in the right premotor gyrus → high-grade primary brain tumour. mx 437 ×2
Slide 19

IMAGING

CT or MRI — Choosing the Right First Study

Choose CT when…

Choose MRI when…

  • Acute deterioration or suspected herniation
  • Trauma work-up
  • Rapid triage in the emergency department
  • MRI is contraindicated (e.g. certain implants) or unavailable
  • Assessing bone involvement / calcification
  • Definitive characterization of a known/suspected tumor
  • Pre-operative surgical planning
  • Assessing posterior fossa or brainstem lesions
  • Following tumor response over time
  • Functional mapping near eloquent cortex

Localization of Intracranial Tumors

18

  • Known prostate cancer, back pain, difficulty walking, thoracic tenderness, impaired proprioception → MRI whole spine (metastatic cord compression; image the whole spine — skip lesions). 439 ×4
  • Known IV drug user, 2 weeks of neck pain + bilateral hand numbness, normal exam → cervical spine MRI (rule out epidural abscess/discitis). 436

Key Takeaways

  • Presentation reflects function: mass effect, infiltration, irritation, or CSF obstruction.
  • Raised ICP has a recognizable syndrome — headache, vomiting, papilledema, and (late) Cushing triad.
  • Each lobe has a signature deficit pattern — use the exam to build an anatomical hypothesis.
  • CT triages acutely; MRI defines and plans around the lesion.
  • Always correlate the clinical localization with imaging before finalizing a surgical plan.

CASE EXAMPLE 1

Frontal Lobe Mass

History

A patient presents with progressive personality change and one witnessed focal motor seizure. MRI was obtained for further work-up.

Examination

  • Mild disinhibition and flattened affect
  • Subtle contralateral pronator drift
  • Non-fluent speech output with preserved comprehension (dominant hemisphere)
  • No visual field deficit

Axial post-contrast T1 MRI: an irregularly enhancing frontal mass with central necrosis and surrounding vasogenic edema.

Personality change + focal seizure + an enhancing frontal mass → localizes to the frontal lobe.

CASE EXAMPLE 2

Posterior Fossa Mass

History

A child presents with several weeks of early-morning headache and vomiting, and a new unsteady, wide-based gait.

Examination

  • Papilledema on fundoscopy
  • Truncal ataxia — unable to tandem walk
  • Dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing
  • No focal limb weakness; cranial nerves intact

Posterior fossa mass

Resulting hydrocephalus

A posterior fossa mass effacing the fourth ventricle, with resulting dilation of the lateral ventricles (obstructive hydrocephalus).

Truncal ataxia + early raised ICP in a child → classic for a posterior fossa tumor causing obstructive hydrocephalus.

Mastery Checklist

1

Four mechanisms: mass effect (can recover after removal), infiltration (cannot be cleanly separated), cortical irritation (seizures), CSF obstruction (hydrocephalus).

2

3

4

History + exam → hypothesis → imaging. Report side + lobe + nearby functional structures — never just “a mass”.

CN VI palsy = classic false localizing sign of raised ICP.

Monro–Kellie: brain 80 / blood 10 / CSF 10. Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration) = late, dangerous sign.

5

Raised ICP: morning headache, worse with cough / strain / lying flat, vomiting, blurred vision, ↓ consciousness. Acute drop: ABC → urgent CT.

6

Seizure clues: frontal = motor jerking + head deviation; temporal = déjà vu + automatisms; parietal = sensory distortion; occipital = flashing lights / visual hallucinations.

7

Frontal: contralateral hemiparesis, Broca (dominant F3), disinhibition / apathy, anosmia, gaze; gait apraxia + urinary incontinence = bifrontal.

8

Parietal: dominant = Gerstmann (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, L–R confusion); non-dominant = contralateral neglect without weakness.

9

Temporal: Wernicke = fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension; left hippocampus = verbal memory, right = non-verbal.

10

Quadrantanopias: parietal → inferior; temporal (Meyer loop) → superior (“pie in the sky”). Occipital → hemianopia with macular sparing; Anton = cortical blindness with denial.

11

Posterior fossa: early obstructive hydrocephalus; vermis = truncal ataxia, hemisphere = limb ataxia / dysmetria; nystagmus, wide-based gait, scanning speech; common in children.

12

Sellar: bitemporal hemianopia; cavernous sinus = ICA + CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI; prolactinoma = menstrual irregularity (F), impotence + low libido (M).

13

CT first for emergencies, trauma, hemorrhage, bone / calcification, or when MRI is contraindicated; MRI for definitive characterization, posterior fossa / brainstem, surgical planning and follow-up.
